blocks.text: 1. overview
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443903696-917767281.png

Confidence, the previous topic, closed with a specific, concrete blind spot identified directly: a rule can show an impressively high confidence value purely because its consequent happens to be extremely common on its own, entirely independent of whatever the antecedent actually is. Lift, the third and final metric in this trio, was built specifically to close that exact gap, correcting Confidence by explicitly comparing it against how often the consequent occurs on its own, its baseline rate, absent any information about the antecedent at all.

With Lift in hand, the full toolkit for scoring an association rule is complete: Support checks that a rule rests on enough real observed data, Confidence checks that the rule is a directionally reliable prediction, and Lift checks that the rule represents a genuine, meaningful association rather than a coincidence driven by one item simply being popular on its own.
2. The Formula
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443903697-867696303.png

For a rule such as bread and butter implies jam, Lift is calculated as the Confidence of that rule divided by the overall support of jam on its own, entirely independent of bread and butter. Written out fully in terms of support alone, this is equivalent to the support of the combined itemset, bread, butter, and jam together, divided by the product of the support of the antecedent, bread and butter, and the support of the consequent, jam, each considered separately.

Lift measures precisely how many times more likely the consequent becomes, given that the antecedent has occurred, compared to the consequent's ordinary, unconditional baseline rate across the entire dataset. This is exactly the correction Confidence alone was missing: instead of just asking how often the consequent follows the antecedent, Lift asks how much more often it follows, compared to how often it would have shown up anyway, with no information about the antecedent at all.
3. Reading a Lift Value
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443903697-876030782.png

Lift values fall into three clean, directly interpretable categories. A lift value greater than 1 indicates a genuine positive association: the presence of the antecedent actually increases the likelihood of the consequent beyond what its baseline popularity alone would predict, exactly the kind of rule worth reporting and acting on. A lift value of exactly 1 indicates no association whatsoever, meaning the antecedent and consequent are statistically independent of each other, the consequent is exactly as likely to occur whether or not the antecedent occurred.

A lift value less than 1 indicates a genuine negative association: the presence of the antecedent actually decreases the likelihood of the consequent below its normal baseline rate, meaning the two items are, in a meaningful statistical sense, somewhat mutually exclusive or substitutable for one another rather than complementary. All three of these categories carry genuine, distinct, useful information for whoever is analyzing the resulting rules.

blocks.text: 4. Revisiting the Misleading Example

It is worth returning directly to the exact misleading scenario raised at the end of the Confidence topic. There, the rule bread and butter implies jam showed a confidence of 0.8, appearing quite strong on its own, but jam's overall baseline support, entirely independent of bread and butter, was already 0.78, since jam happened to be an extremely popular item purchased in the vast majority of all transactions regardless.

Computing Lift for this rule gives 0.8 divided by 0.78, which comes out to approximately 1.03, a lift value barely above 1. This immediately reveals what raw confidence alone had obscured: this rule adds almost no genuine additional predictive information beyond simply knowing how popular jam already is on its own. A lift this close to 1 is a clear, quantitative signal to treat this particular rule with real skepticism, despite its impressive-looking 80 percent confidence value.
5. A Genuinely Strong Association
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443903698-667518566.png

For contrast, consider a different rule: diapers implies beer, a famously cited illustrative example in association rule mining folklore, with a confidence of 0.6. Suppose beer's overall baseline support, independent of diapers, is comparatively low, only 0.1 across the whole dataset. Computing Lift here gives 0.6 divided by 0.1, which equals 6.0, a substantially strong lift value.

A lift of 6 means customers who bought diapers were six times more likely to also buy beer than an entirely random shopper drawn from the full customer base would have been. This is a genuinely strong, surprising, and directly actionable association, exactly the kind of pattern the whole point of association rule mining is designed to surface, standing in sharp contrast to the barely-above-baseline bread-butter-jam rule from the previous section.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The diapers-and-beer example is a well-known, often-retold anecdote in the association rule mining literature, illustrating exactly the kind of surprising, non-obvious, high-lift pattern this technique was originally built to uncover in real retail transaction data.

blocks.text: 6. Lift Is Symmetric
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443903698-779462284.png

Confidence, covered in the previous topic, is explicitly directional: confidence of A implies B generally differs from confidence of B implies A. Lift behaves quite differently in this respect. Lift of A implies B is always exactly equal to lift of B implies A, with no exceptions, a direct mathematical consequence of its formula.

Written as support of A and B together divided by the product of support of A alone and support of B alone, the formula treats A and B in a completely symmetric, interchangeable way, since multiplication does not care about order. This means Lift measures the strength of the association between two items as a pure, symmetric fact about how those two items relate to each other, entirely independent of which one happens to be framed as the antecedent, or trigger, and which as the consequent, or predicted outcome, in a particular directional rule.
7. Negative Lift Is Useful Information Too

blocks.alt: Negative Lift Is Useful Information Too
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443904500-38129615.png

A lift value below 1 is sometimes overlooked in practice, since the natural instinct is to search for strong positive associations worth acting on. But a genuinely negative association is real, useful information in its own right. Consider a hypothetical rule sunscreen implies umbrella with a computed lift of 0.4, meaning customers who buy sunscreen are noticeably less likely than an average shopper to also buy an umbrella in that same transaction, a perfectly sensible pattern given sunny weather tends to call for one item and not the other.

Recognizing and reporting these negative associations matters for the exact same reasons positive ones do: they reveal real structure in customer behavior, and depending on the business context, they can inform decisions just as directly as a positive association would, for instance by suggesting these two product categories should not be jointly promoted together, or that separate, tailored marketing messages make more sense for each.
8. The Complete Pipeline

With Lift now covered, the full standard association rule mining pipeline, built up across the last four topics, is complete. Frequent itemsets are first mined using either Apriori or FP-Growth, filtered by a minimum support threshold, exactly as covered in their own dedicated topics. Candidate directional rules are then generated from each of those frequent itemsets, as first described in the Apriori Algorithm topic.

Those candidate rules are filtered a second time using a minimum confidence threshold, keeping only the directionally reliable ones, exactly the process covered in the Confidence topic. Finally, the surviving rules are filtered or ranked using Lift, typically keeping only those with a lift meaningfully greater than 1, ensuring the final reported rules are not just frequent and directionally reliable, but also represent a genuine, non-trivial association worth someone's actual attention.

blocks.text: 9. Lift's Own Limitations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443904502-621872463.png

Lift is not without its own caveats. It can be quite sensitive to rare items: a combination involving an item that appears in only a handful of transactions overall can occasionally produce an extremely high lift value purely from a small number of coincidental co-occurrences, exactly the same statistical reliability concern the Support topic raised, now reappearing in a slightly different form. This is exactly why Support should always be checked alongside Lift, never relied upon in isolation, since a high lift resting on a tiny support value is not a trustworthy signal on its own.

Lift also carries no direct sense of practical magnitude or business impact on its own; a lift of 6 says nothing by itself about how many actual transactions, or how much real revenue, that particular rule represents, which is precisely why it is used as a final filter or ranking signal alongside Support, rather than the sole metric relied upon in isolation. A rule with high lift but very low support might be a statistical curiosity rather than a genuinely actionable business insight.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A common, sound practical rule of thumb: report and act on rules only when they clear reasonable thresholds on all three metrics simultaneously, adequate Support, adequate Confidence, and Lift meaningfully above 1, rather than optimizing for any single one of the three in isolation.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below computes Lift for several candidate rules and identifies which ones represent genuinely strong associations versus ones that are merely riding on a popular consequent.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import apriori, association_rules
from mlxtend.preprocessing import TransactionEncoder

transactions = [
    ["bread", "butter", "jam"], ["bread", "butter"], ["bread", "milk"],
    ["bread", "butter", "jam", "milk"], ["butter", "jam"], ["bread", "butter", "milk"],
    ["bread", "milk"], ["butter", "jam"], ["bread", "butter", "jam"], ["bread", "jam"],
    ["diapers", "beer"], ["diapers", "beer", "chips"], ["diapers", "milk"], ["beer", "chips"],
]

encoder = TransactionEncoder()
encoded_array = encoder.fit(transactions).transform(transactions)
df = pd.DataFrame(encoded_array, columns=encoder.columns_)

frequent_itemsets = apriori(df, min_support=0.1, use_colnames=True)
rules = association_rules(frequent_itemsets, metric="lift", min_threshold=0.0)

rules_sorted = rules.sort_values('lift', ascending=False)
print("All rules ranked by Lift:")
print(rules_sorted[['antecedents', 'consequents', 'support', 'confidence', 'lift']].to_string(index=False))

strong_rules = rules[(rules['lift'] > 1.5) & (rules['support'] >= 0.1)]
print(f"\nGenuinely strong, well-supported rules (lift > 1.5, support >= 0.1): {len(strong_rules)}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Sorting by Lift, rather than Confidence, surfaces the diapers-and-beer style rules as the most genuinely interesting associations in this small dataset, exactly the kind of surprising, non-obvious pattern this whole three-metric pipeline was built to find.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Lift corrects Confidence by dividing it by the consequent's own baseline support, independent of the antecedent.
Lift greater than 1 means positive association; exactly 1 means independence; less than 1 means negative association.
A rule with high confidence but a lift near 1 adds little real predictive value beyond the consequent's own popularity.
A rule with a lift well above 1 represents a genuinely strong, surprising, actionable association.
Unlike Confidence, Lift is symmetric: lift of A implies B always equals lift of B implies A exactly.
A lift below 1 reveals a genuine negative association, useful information in its own right, not just noise.
The complete pipeline mines itemsets by Support, generates rules, filters by Confidence, then filters or ranks by Lift.
Lift can be distorted by rare items and carries no sense of practical magnitude, so it should always be checked alongside Support.
